sources.citation: Greenhill, Simon J., Robert Blust & Russell D. Gray (eds.). 2008-. Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database, entry 1392 'Hote (Misim dialect)' [ISO hot, Glottocode hote1245], 190 items; sources: (1) Malcolm Ross, fieldnotes; (2) Marguerite Muzzey, n.d., Electronic dictionary of Hote, Ukarumpa: SIL. Typed and checked by Malcolm Ross.
sources.note: no phonology content: orthographic basic-vocabulary list with cognacy coding; no stress marks or prosodic notes on the entry page.

sources.citation: Muzzey, Marguerite. 1988. Hote Phonology Essentials. Ukarumpa: SIL. Ms., 55 pp. (SIL archives 56480) - Introduction p. 1 and STRESS section pp. 41-42
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: p. 1: 'Hote is a family consisting of three dialects--Hote, Yamap, and Misim--spoken in eighteen villages. McElhanon, 1984, referred to these three dialects as closely related languages. Field work commenced in December of 1976, in Yemli village' (Yemli = Hote dialect proper). The STRESS section (pp. 41-42, already quoted in the hote1245 record) gives first-syllable stress with listed exceptions for the Hote dialect; no Yamap-specific data or remark on dialect differences in stress.

sources.citation: Muzzey, Marguerite. 1979. Hote Grammar Essentials. Ukarumpa: SIL. Ms., 101 pp. (SIL archives 56481) - Introduction p. 1
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: p. 1: 'It is an isolate consisting of three dialects--Hote, Yamap, and Missim--spoken in eighteen villages.. Data for this paper was collected during nine months' residence in the village of Yemli'. Sec. 1.1 stress patterns (p. 7) describe Hote (Yemli) only.

sources.citation: Yamap NT+ : Portions of the Holy Bible in the Yamap language of Papua New Guinea / Buk Baibel long tokples Yamap long Niugini (Matthew, Mark, Luke). 2025. Ukarumpa: SIL Papua New Guinea; contributors Papua New Guinea Bible Translation Association and The Seed Company. eBible.org id ymp (YMPSIL), source files dated 2025-07-10, CC BY-SA 4.0.
sources.note: no phonology content: scripture text only (MAT, MRK, LUK chapters + copyright page; no introduction, alphabet or pronunciation guide in the HTML edition). The practical orthography uses ê, ô, ŋ and no accent or tone marks - orthographic data, not a statement.

sources.citation: Hammarstrom, Harald & Sebastian Nordhoff. 2012. Online appendix to 'The languages of Melanesia: quantifying the level of coverage'. In Nicholas Evans & Marian Klamer (eds.), Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia: challenges for the 21st century (Language Documentation & Conservation Special Publication 5), 13-34. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. hdl:10125/4559 (appendix PDF, c. 950 pp.)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Melanesia-wide coverage bibliography (one entry per language listing its most extensive descriptive sources with type tags); entry lists only Smith 1988 Morobe counting systems [overview, minimal] (Brownie ed. 2000 DP 46 listed under the Misim-Yamap node); no phonology or grammar recorded for this language and no stress or tone content anywhere in the entry.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 1991. Sound change and migration distance. In Robert Blust (ed.), Currents in Pacific linguistics: Papers on Austronesian languages and ethnolinguistics in honour of George W. Grace, 27-42. Pacific Linguistics C-117. Canberra: Australian National University. (hdl:1885/253742)
sources.note: no phonology content beyond one segmental datum: under 'EY = 0.5: 1) [p]/[v]' the list '(Gitua, Piu, Kapin, Mumeng, Mapos Buang, Manga Buang, Yehes, Hote, Yamap, Misim, Kaiwa..)' records that Yamap reflects *p as p/v. The strings stress/Stress/accent/tone/penult do not occur in the text ('tonal' once, in a reference title on Chamic; 'syllable' once, about PAn canonical shape).

sources.citation: Muzzey, Marguerite. 1989. Orthography paper, Hote language. Ukarumpa: SIL ms. (SIL archives item 56450)
sources.note: Muzzey treats Yamap as a Hote dialect; an orthography paper for the whole 'Hote family' might note dialect differences including stress. Not downloaded.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm D. 1988. Proto Oceanic and the Austronesian languages of western Melanesia. Pacific Linguistics C-98. Canberra: ANU. 502 pp.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201.R67 1988)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201 .R67 1988
sources.note: Comparative work only. Yamap appears as 'Hote (Yamap)' in cognate sets, data from Hooley 1971 (source table p. 406); classification pp. 133-134 lists 'Hote (inc. Misim and Yamap dialects)'; fn. 55 (p. 418): 'I have treated Hote, Misim and Yamap as dialects of a single language on the basis of comments by Muzzey (1979) and by my informant.' The only stress remark is historical (p. 157): 'Unstressed vowels were deleted or became a non-phonemic schwa.. in Proto Hote/Buang, creating consonant clusters' - no synchronic statement of stress placement for Yamap or Hote.

sources.citation: Smith, Geoffrey P. 1988. Morobe counting systems. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 26, 1-132. Pacific Linguistics A-76. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Entry '40. YAMAP' (p. 75): numerals 1-20 (tom, yi, lu, va, vagem vi..) from an informant in Lae from Bodadum village; 'incomplete information'. No phonology and nothing on stress; the word 'stress' occurs only in the non-linguistic sense.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1984. A linguistic field guide to the Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-57. Canberra: ANU. 72 pp.
sources.note: Language census only: Hote Family = 36 Hote, 39 Misim, 40 Yamap, 'three closely related languages' (p. 14); '(40) Yamap (pop. 1,310)' at Bodabu (337), Doli (243), Pilimung (404), Yasingli (286) (p. 21); SIL team for 'Hote / Yamap-Hote-Musin' at Yemli = Muzzey (p. 16). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Capell, A. 1976. General picture of Austronesian languages, New Guinea area. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 5-52. Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: no phonology content for Yamap; general typological survey of New Guinea Austronesian languages.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. 1976. Austronesian languages: Morobe Province. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 335-348. Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: no phonology content: classification, cognate percentages and a call for fieldwork only; the words stress/accent/tone do not occur.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. 1976. History of research in Austronesian languages: Morobe Province. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 115-128. Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: Australian National University. (hdl:1885/252990)
sources.note: no phonology content for Yamap: research history only. Sec. 4.2.4.2 'Descriptive studies' names work on Yabem, Tami, Wampar, Sio, Adzera, Central Buang, Manga Buang, Patep and the lower Watut languages; the only prosodic remark concerns other languages ('tone is a phonemic feature of Yabem, Bakaua, and Tami (Capell 1949; Wurm 1954). The author has observed that Labu also displays this feature'); conclusion: 'The principal needs are for more in-depth studies of individual languages'. Hote/Yamap/Misim occur nowhere in the text (checked on the despaced text).

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. 1971. Austronesian languages of the Morobe District, Papua New Guinea. Oceanic Linguistics 10(2): 79-151.
sources.note: Glottolog's most extensive description of Yamap and the only primary Yamap data source used by Ross 1988; a survey wordlist that may carry phonetic transcription with stress marks but probably no stress rule.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. & K. A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District - New Guinea. In S. A. Wurm & D. C. Laycock (eds.), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell, 1065-1094. Pacific Linguistics C-13. Canberra: Australian National University.
